150	
151	**The beacon override**: a call site within four lines of a `SAFETY`,
152	`CRITICAL` or `INVARIANT` comment is pinned to the top of the docket whatever
153	it scored, with the comment shown. Someone wrote that note by hand; it outranks
154	a heuristic.
155	
156	**The scar factor** is opt in with `--history` and multiplies by up to 2 for a
157	file with several recent fix commits. It is off by default because it is noisy.
158	
159	Ties break by file path then symbol name, so two runs on one checkpoint produce
160	the same order.
161	
162	## The sweep
163	
164	After the selected tests, the whole suite runs once by default. Every test that
165	changed state but was not selected is reported as a leak with the reason the
166	selection missed it: a path deeper than the search went, no resolved call edges
167	from the test file, a path only over a relation Umbra does not traverse, or
168	nothing the graph can see. The count is printed even when it is zero, because a
169	selection that audits itself is worth more than one that does not. `--no-audit`
170	skips it and the header says the selection is unaudited.
171	
172	## Security
173	
174	- Umbra runs as the invoking user and asks for nothing more. It sees exactly
175	  what you can see through git and the Entire CLI.
176	- **No transcript prose reaches any output**, with one named exception: the
177	  "session said" sentence, taken from Entire's stored checkpoint summary or, if
178	  there is none, the agent's own last sentence. It is scrubbed and capped at
179	  200 characters, and it is displayed, never verified.
180	- **Umbra never runs a command it found in a transcript.** Test ids are built
181	  from graph data, validated against `^[A-Za-z0-9_./:\[\]\-]+$`, and passed as
182	  separate argv elements. There is no `sh -c` anywhere in Umbra.
183	- The runner comes only from `--test`. Umbra echoes the full command before
184	  running it, and everything runs in detached worktrees, never in your working
185	  tree.
186	- The report is one self-contained file with a Content-Security-Policy that
187	  forbids external scripts, styles, images and connections. It makes no
188	  requests. The drop-in viewer on the landing page reads files in your browser
189	  and uploads nothing.
190	- Reports name symbols, files and spans inside the blast radius. Share one with
191	  the same care you would share a diff.
192	
193	## Limitations
194	
195	- Read evidence is file and line-range based. A mention in the agent's text is
196	  attention, not reading, and is ranked as the weakest tier.
197	- Graph edges are not complete: reflection, dynamic dispatch and configuration
198	  are invisible, so umbra is a **lower bound** on what was unexamined. The
199	  sweep's leak reasons are how a reader sees the gap.
200	- Fault lines and beacons are matched by a regular expression window around the
201	  call-site line, not by a parser.
202	- Ranking weights are hand set and printed. They are a heuristic, not a
203	  measurement.
204	- Scrubbing of command prefixes and failure excerpts is pattern based.
205	- One transcript adapter, for Claude Code. An agent whose transcript carries no
206	  tool records gets the unknown state.
207	- A destructive `--test` runner does what it says. The echo before execution is
208	  the only guard.
209	- **Worktrees are keyed by commit in a shared directory, so two checkouts of
210	  one repository collide on one worktree.** They are removed on exit unless
211	  `--keep-worktrees` was passed, but a run that died before its cleanup, or a
212	  checkout that has since been deleted, leaves one behind. A leftover is now
213	  reused only when it is a healthy checkout sitting at the wanted commit, and
214	  otherwise removed and pruned first, which covers the deleted-checkout case.
215	  What it does not cover is a healthy worktree belonging to a different
216	  checkout of the same repository: that one is reused, and it carries the other
217	  checkout's `.git` link with it, so if that checkout sits somewhere Graph
218	  refuses to run the failure lands in the run that did nothing wrong. There is
219	  no `umbra clean` command; `SECURITY_AND_ACCESS.md` describes one and it was
220	  never built. Delete them by hand:
221	
222	  ```
223	  rm -rf "$ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR/wt"                  # managed install
224	  rm -rf "${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/umbra/wt"    # otherwise
225	  ```
226	
227	  Under a managed install that first path is usually
228	  `~/.local/share/entire/plugins/data/umbra/wt`.
229	- **A check that has never been observed to fail is not yet a check.** Four
230	  verifications in this build returned a confident pass that was wrong: local
231	  tests green on a repository a clone could not build, a cracked-probe count
232	  that named a test outside the selection, a commit check that counted `ok`
233	  lines instead of looking for `FAIL`, and a refs audit that reported thirty
234	  refs of zero bytes because `git ls-tree` is scoped to the working directory.
235	  The clearest case had no symptom at all: all four label-placement tests are
236	  built on `Box.Overlaps`, and making it return false for every pair left every
237	  one of them passing, across all eight scenarios. They had been proving
238	  determinism, not collision. Every check named in this README now has a test
239	  that plants what the check is for and asserts it fires, and each of those was
240	  proved by mutating the code it checks until it failed. That is the standard;
241	  it is not a guarantee that nothing else here is passing for the wrong reason.
242	- The examined set is built from the session's tool activity. An agent that
243	  reads and edits through shell commands rather than through file tools leaves
244	  no read or edit event, so its work looks unexamined. Umbra found this in its
245	  own build; the report is in `umbra/site/self/`. Every report now carries a
246	  coverage line saying how many of the session's events were file reads and how
247	  many were shell commands, so a thin report can be told from a real finding.
248	- **The report's script is about 1215 lines against a design target of 700,**
249	  and its stylesheet about 480 against 400. Three things account for almost all
250	  of the excess and none of them were foreseen when the target was set: the
251	  attention replay carries a second implementation of the classifier, because
252	  the map has to be reconstructed at any point in the session and that means
253	  the state rules exist in Go and again in the browser; the day scheme and the
254	  print block are a second and third set of rules for the light field, since
255	  removing a glow on a light ground reads as more light rather than less; and
256	  the node shapes are drawn per state and per penumbra tier so the four states
257	  survive greyscale. The duplication of the classifier is the part worth
258	  regretting, and it is guarded rather than trusted: a test feeds eight
259	  recorded scenarios through both implementations at three playhead positions
260	  each and compares every state, tier and announcement.
261	
262	## Not built, and why
263	
264	Adapters for other agents (they get the unknown state, which is correct for a
265	transcript with no tool records). Subagent transcripts. Live mode during a
266	session and a blind-spot budget gate (shadow-branch data is not documented
267	output). Mutability analysis of callees (nothing in the documented surface
268	provides it). Coverage deltas (needs coverage tooling in the target
269	repository). Trend dashboards. Cross-repository dependents. And Umbra never
270	writes code: it shows the shadow, it does not fix it.
271	
272	## Corrections to the design documents
273	
274	Five places where the four planning documents in `umbra/docs/` describe
275	something the installed tools do not do. All five were forced by real output,
276	none by preference. The documents are the original design and are left as
277	written; these are the corrections the code carries.
278	
279	1. **The checkpoint trailer is not hexadecimal.** ARCHITECTURE.md section 1
280	   describes `Entire-Checkpoint: <12 hex>`. The installed CLI writes a 26
281	   character ULID, for example `01M1PVD1WBK1J1J8GWDNJJR7XZ`. A hex-only pattern
282	   matched nothing, so every commit fell through to the session-window fallback
283	   while reporting, wrongly, that it carried no trailer. The pattern now takes
284	   alphanumeric ids of 6 to 40 characters, which covers the ULID, the 12 hex id
285	   of imported history and the 40 hex id of a carry-forward entry.
286	
287	2. **`pytest -q` cannot be verified.** PRD.md uses it in the command surface
288	   and in the demo. Quiet mode prints no per-test ids, so `graph verify`
289	   answers `output format not recognised` and records zero results. The default
290	   is now `pytest -v`, and the table says `add -v` when a baseline comes back
291	   exit-code only.
292	
293	3. **Flags after the reference were silently dropped.** The surface in PRD.md
294	   is `entire umbra <ref> [flags]`, but Go's flag package stops parsing at the
295	   first non-flag argument, so `entire umbra HEAD --run none` ignored
296	   `--run none` and then failed asking for a test runner. Argv is reordered
297	   before parsing, with boolean flags handled so they do not swallow the
298	   reference.
299	
300	4. **`graph checkpoint` answers about the wrong commit when the pairing was a
301	   guess.** ARCHITECTURE.md calls it the documented bridge between Graph and
302	   Checkpoints, and `LoadSources` tried it first. It returns the changes of the
303	   commit *that checkpoint belongs to*. When a reference is paired with a
304	   checkpoint by session window, that is a guess about which session produced
305	   the commit and says nothing about which commit the checkpoint owns. This
306	   never showed here, because the pairing happens to choose an imported
307	   checkpoint that owns no commit and the fallback runs. In a clone it chose a
308	   hook-written checkpoint that does own one, and the report described that
309	   commit's changes under the header of the one the reader asked for: the
310	   header said `1c2cf29` while the sources were the transcript package from
311	   phase 3. The bridge is now used only when the reference resolved through the
312	   trailer or through the checkpoint id, where the two are the same work.
313	
314	5. **A stale worktree poisoned every later run.** Worktrees are keyed by commit
315	   under a shared data directory, so two checkouts of one repository, or a run
316	   that died before its cleanup, collide on one path. The code reused anything
317	   with a `.git` in it. A worktree left behind by a checkout that had since
318	   been deleted made git unable to read its metadata and Graph refuse to run
319	   there, for every subsequent run against that commit from any checkout. A
320	   leftover is now reused only when it is a healthy checkout sitting at the
321	   wanted commit, and otherwise removed and pruned first. The residual case is
322	   in the limitations above.
323	
324	Corrections 4 and 5 were both found by the end-to-end tests failing in a fresh
325	clone after passing here, which is the same lesson as the `.gitignore` below.
326	
327	Two smaller ones, for completeness. Entire has more than one wording for an
328	absent summary, so any fully italicised summary block is treated as absent. And
329	`graph impact --format json` carries `call_site.line` and `additional_sites`
330	directly, so it is the primary path and the text parser the design sketched is
331	the fallback, still tested.
332	
333	## The final review
334	
335	Phase 11 was a semantic-diff review of the whole build to that point,
336	comparing the first commit against the last:
337	
338	```
339	entire graph diff --base 2495309553ee8c01a61a3c4922e45861d3d4de6d --head HEAD --repo .
340	```
341	
342	The diff itself is unremarkable: 1014 added entities, no signature changes, and
343	no function without an incoming edge, which is what a build that only ever added
344	code should look like. The interesting part was what the diff did not contain,
345	and it is the single most useful thing Graph did in this build.
346	
347	### The .gitignore that hid the command package
348	
349	Reading the diff, `umbra/cmd` was missing. Not thin, not partial: the graph had
350	no symbols for it at all, while it had 1014 for everything else. A directory of
351	Go files that the build had been compiling and testing for nine phases was, as
352	far as Graph could see, not there.
353	
354	Graph builds its snapshot from the repository, and it honours `.gitignore`. So
355	the question was not what Graph had failed to parse. It was what git had been
356	told to ignore. The answer was the second line of a `.gitignore` I wrote myself
357	in the first commit, under a heading that says exactly what I meant it to do:
358	
359	```
360	# Go build output
361	entire-umbra
362	```
363	
364	I meant that to ignore the compiled binary, which is written as `entire-umbra`.
365	A gitignore pattern with no slash in it is not anchored to the repository root
366	and does not distinguish a file from a directory: it matches any path component
367	with that name, at any depth. The binary is called `entire-umbra`. So is the
368	directory the binary's source lives in. The pattern matched
369	`umbra/cmd/entire-umbra/` and everything under it.
370	
371	`git ls-files umbra/cmd/` returned nothing. `main.go`, `analyze.go`,
372	`execute.go`, `options.go`, `output.go`, `record.go` and `options_test.go` had
373	never been committed. The command package went in during phase 2 and was
374	untracked through phase 10, nine phases in which every commit message reported
375	a rising test count that included tests in a file the repository did not have.
376	
377	Nothing caught it, and nothing was going to. `go build ./...` and
378	`go test ./...` read the working tree, and the files were on disk, so they were
379	green throughout and told me nothing. `git status` says nothing about a path it
380	has been told to ignore. `git commit -a` does not add an ignored file. The only
381	symptom available to me was one I never looked at: a clone.
382	
383	The fix was to anchor the patterns to the paths the binaries are actually
384	written to, so a directory name can never collide with them again:
385	
386	```
387	/entire-umbra
388	/umbra/entire-umbra
389	/umbra-out/
390	```
391	
392	The seven files were then committed, and the thing that should have been done
393	long before was done at last:
394	
395	```
396	git clone . /tmp/clone && cd /tmp/clone/umbra
397	go build ./...   # OK
398	go test ./...    # every package ok
399	```
400	
401	That clone is the verification. Before the fix it would have failed to build,
402	because `package main` did not exist in the repository. After it, it builds and
403	every test passes, which is the only evidence that means anything here.
404	
405	This is the clearest case in the build of Graph driving a decision rather than
406	confirming one. Nothing else in the toolchain was looking at the repository.
407	The compiler, the test runner and my own reading were all looking at the
408	working tree, where the code was present and correct. Graph was looking at what
409	had actually been committed, and the gap between those two things was an entire
410	package. A green test run is not the same as a correct repository, and it takes
411	a tool that reads the repository to tell you which one you have.
412	
413	### The self report
414	
415	Then Umbra was run on the session that built it. On the commit where it changed
416	its own `shadow.Build`, all twelve dependents came back umbra, including every
417	scenario test. That reading is correct, and the reason is the most useful thing
418	this project learned about itself: the change was made with a shell command
419	rather than the editing tool, so the session produced no read and no edit event
420	for that file. **Umbra's examined set is built from tool activity, so an agent
421	that edits through the shell leaves no trace Umbra can see.** It is the same
422	shape of blind spot the product exists to find, pointed at the product. The
423	report is in `umbra/site/self/`.
424	
425	Running the report on itself also found two bugs in the scrubber, both fixed:
426	paths from outside the repository were reaching the timeline through search
427	output, and the base64 heuristic was redacting git object ids and worktree
428	paths, which is exactly the text a reader needs in order to check a line.
429	
430	## Development record
431	
432	Umbra was built in a standalone repository, `u7k4rs6/Umbra`, rather than inside
433	a fork of `entireio/entire-graph`. The `umbra/` layout from ARCHITECTURE.md was
434	preserved exactly so the module can be grafted into a fork without moving a
435	file, and `scripts/graft.sh` does that graft, with a dry run, without pushing.
436	The build's own checkpoint trail lives in this repository under
437	`refs/entire/checkpoints/`, and the phase by phase record is the table at the
438	top of [umbra/NOTES.md](umbra/NOTES.md), which covers all seventeen phases and
439	carries what each one found and where the design documents turned out to be
440	wrong.
441	
442	Seventeen phases, of which the first thirteen built the product. The last four
443	were not features:
444	
445	- **14** replaced the landing page's scripted sample with a real run, added a
446	  second map from an imported session in another project, and prepared two
447	  scripts that were deliberately not executed: the graft, and a read-only audit
448	  of what the checkpoint refs on the remote contain.
449	- **15** made the scrubber the only exit. Five leaks had been the same bug five
450	  times, an output path that wrote without scrubbing, so the renderers now take
451	  a value that only the scrubbing path can produce. It also gave every check in
452	  the project a test that proves the check can fail.
453	- **16** restyled the landing page around a drawn eclipse. No raster asset and
454	  no request for one: the corona is inline SVG built deterministically from the
455	  report's own numbers.
456	- **17** is this pass: two visual checks decided from screenshots rather than
457	  from the CSS, [umbra/PUBLISH.md](umbra/PUBLISH.md), and the verification of
458	  this README against the repository.
459	
460	[umbra/PUBLISH.md](umbra/PUBLISH.md) is a checklist for the sitting in which
461	this repository is made public. Nothing in it has been run.
462	
463	**Which maps are which.** The landing page shows two, and they are not the same
464	kind of thing.
465	
466	- The first is a **real session on a seeded fixture**. The session, its tool
467	  activity and the test results are real: checkpoint `b20f84567474` against
468	  commit `1c2cf29`, where an agent changed a signature and five probes cracked.
469	  What is arranged is the fixture underneath it, `umbra/fixtures/app`, which was
470	  written to have callers a session would plausibly miss. The sentence above the
471	  map is the agent's own, taken from the stored transcript.
472	- The second is **not seeded at all**: a real session from another project of
473	  the builder's, imported with `entire import` and analysed unchanged. Every one
474	  of the four symbols that depend on what it changed came back umbra. Nothing
475	  about it was arranged, including the result.
476	
477	**Nothing on the page is scripted.** There is no map drawn from an invented
478	report. Until phase 14 there was one: the sample was assembled by the site
479	generator, with a checkpoint id of `sample000class`, a commit of all zeros and a
480	session sentence written by hand, under a caption calling it a real report. It
481	was replaced by a real run, and the generator now refuses a report carrying
482	those markers so the caption cannot drift away from the file again.
483	
484	The eight scenarios under `umbra/fixtures/recorded/` are **authored
485	transcripts**, written to exercise one classifier rule each. They drive tests
486	and are never rendered as a map on the page. `umbra/fixtures/recorded/minimal/`
487	is different: a full recording of a real short session, hand reviewed before it
488	was committed.
489	
490	## Prior work and AI disclosure
491	
492	No code was reused. The idea of subtracting the examined set from a blast
493	radius was developed in planning for this event.
494	
495	All product code across all seventeen phases was written during the build with
496	an AI coding agent, captured in Entire checkpoints. That includes the tests, the
497	landing page, the corona renderer and every document in this repository except
498	the four planning documents in `umbra/docs/`, which were written before the
499	build with AI assistance and are the first commit.
500	
501	What came from the human rather than the agent: the problem, the four settled
502	decisions in the kickoff, the scope of each phase, the decision to keep the
503	repository private, and the visual direction for the landing page in phase 16,
504	which was specified before it was built and not proposed by the agent. Every
505	phase was reviewed and accepted by hand before the next one started.
506	
507	`umbra/NOTES.md` records what the probe found, which degradations are in
508	effect, the places the design documents turned out to be wrong about the
509	installed tools, and the mistakes: the four confident wrong answers, the five
510	scrubbing leaks, and the label tests that were proving nothing. Those are in
511	there because a build record that only lists what worked is not a record.
512	
513	## Layout
514	
515	```
516	umbra/
517	  cmd/entire-umbra/     flags, wiring, exit codes
518	  internal/runner/      the one boundary to external processes, and its replay
519	  internal/checkpoint/  resolve, worktrees, transcript fetch
520	  internal/transcript/  normalized events; the Claude Code adapter
521	  internal/graph/       snapshot, relations, BFS, impact, commit, verify
522	  internal/shadow/      examined set, classifier, ranker, selection, forensics
523	  internal/report/      table, json, layout, html, packet
524	  fixtures/app/         the seeded Python service
525	  fixtures/recorded/    the eight scenarios, plus one real minimal recording
526	  scripts/              the graft and the read-only checkpoint refs audit
527	  site/                 landing page, the corona renderer, the drop-in viewer
528	  docs/                 the four planning documents, and docs/renders/
529	  NOTES.md              the phase by phase build record
530	  PUBLISH.md            the checklist for making this repository public
531	```
532	
533	Built during Bengaluru Tech Week on the Entire ecosystem.
534

# Umbra

**Umbra finds the code an AI agent's change affects but the agent never looked at.**

It is a plugin for the [Entire CLI](https://github.com/entireio/cli), run as
`entire umbra <checkpoint>`. It takes the dependents of every changed symbol
from [Entire Graph](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph), subtracts what
the session actually examined according to the checkpoint's tool activity and
the agent's own words, ranks what is left in shadow, runs the tests that reach
it, and then sweeps the whole suite once so the selection audits itself.

The report is an eclipse map you can replay in the order the agent looked at
things, plus a one-page packet a reviewer reads in a minute.

The core is deterministic and offline. **There is no model anywhere in Umbra.**

## Who it is for

The reviewer of an agent-authored change, who wants to know where to look
first. A clean diff and a confident description tell you what changed. They do
not tell you what the agent never opened.

The everyday case: a signature change on `compute_total`, seven callers, three
of them tests in a file the session never opened, committed with a message that
says the callers were checked because only one test file ran.

```
Umbra  01M1PVD1WBK1J1J8GWDNJJR7XZ  1c2cf29  claude-code  depth 2
session said  "Checked the callers and updated them; all tests pass."
compute_total  signature changed  app/service.py:20
light  ●●◐◐◐○○○○○○   2 lit  3 penumbra  6 umbra  0 unknown   18% examined

!◐  apply_refund        app/refunds.py:17      direct caller  depth 1  echo fault line beacon  10.5
    # SAFETY: a pricing failure must not refund the full amount paid.
 ○  test_rounding       tests/test_service.py:7  direct caller  depth 1  test far field   12.0  fail
 ○  test_negative       tests/test_service.py:13 direct caller  depth 1  test far field   12.0  fail

probes  8 selected  5 cracked
sweep   full suite  0 leaks
```

## The four states

| State | Glyph | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Lit | ● | Read with a range covering the symbol, at or after the change began; or edited |
| Penumbra | ◐ | Half seen: `glance`, `glimpse`, `quoted`, `afterimage` or `echo` |
| Umbra | ○ | Nothing in the session touched or mentioned the file |
| Unknown | ? | The transcript carries no tool events and no mentions |

Missing data is a state, never an error. A transcript with no tool records
gives every node the unknown state, which is the correct answer rather than a
guess, and the selection falls back to the graph alone.

## Install

```
go install github.com/u7k4rs6/Umbra/umbra/cmd/entire-umbra@main
```

Any executable named `entire-<name>` on `$PATH` is dispatched by the Entire CLI
kubectl style, so this is all the installation there is. Requires the Entire
CLI with Checkpoints enabled and the entire-graph plugin.

## Run

```
entire umbra HEAD --test "pytest -v" --out ./umbra-out
open ./umbra-out/umbra.html
```

Use `pytest -v`, not `pytest -q`. Quiet mode prints no per-test names, so
`entire graph verify` cannot tell you which test broke and the verdict degrades
to a suite-level pass or fail. Umbra says so in the header when that happens.

```
entire umbra <checkpoint-id | commit-ish> [flags]

  --test CMD        test runner prefix; validated test ids are appended as argv
  --run none|shadow|all    which selected tests to run (default shadow)
  --no-audit        skip the full-suite sweep, which is on by default
  --history         add the opt-in scar factor from git history
  --depth 1|2|3     dependency hops (default 2)
  --format table|json|html|packet
  --out PATH        write umbra.json, umbra.html and umbra.packet.md
  --fail-on umbra|penumbra|failure|leak    exit 2 when the condition holds
  --snippets        include declaration lines in the report (off by default)
  --all             list lit nodes in the table instead of counting them
  --test-root PATH  where the runner runs, when the project is nested
```

Exit codes: 0 completed, 2 the `--fail-on` condition was met, 1 runtime error.

## Reproduce the demo

```
git clone https://github.com/u7k4rs6/Umbra && cd Umbra
cd umbra/fixtures/app && ./setup.sh && cd ../../..
. umbra/fixtures/app/.venv/bin/activate
entire umbra 1c2cf29 --test "pytest -v"
```

That reports 8 probes selected and 5 cracked, naming `test_empty_is_zero`,
`test_negative` and `test_rounding` in `tests/test_service.py` and both refund
tests in `tests/test_refunds.py`, with a full sweep and 0 leaks.

**The runner has to be on `PATH`, which is why the venv is activated.** Umbra
runs the tests in a detached worktree of the commit, not in your working tree,
so a runner given as a path relative to the repository root does not resolve
from there, and the virtualenv is not in the worktree at all because it is not
committed. A runner that cannot start produces no output, and `verify` then has
nothing to parse: the verdict degrades to a suite-level pass or fail and no
test is named. That looks exactly like the `pytest -q` failure and has a
different cause. Activating the venv, or giving an absolute path to the
interpreter, avoids both.

`entire umbra` has to be installed first, from the Install section above. The
clone also has to sit somewhere Graph will run: Graph refuses git subprocesses
against repository metadata it considers unsafe, which in practice means a
clone under a shared temporary directory fails before any analysis happens.
A clone under your home directory works. This was checked from a fresh clone
rather than assumed, and both readings are in the limitations below.

The fixture is seeded. It is built to produce lit, penumbra and umbra nodes and
a signature change that breaks tests in two files the session never opened. The
report says so and so does this README.

The states you get will not match the example at the top of this README, and
that is correct. Node states come from the examined set, which comes from
whichever checkpoint the reference pairs with, and imported checkpoint history
is local to a machine and is not pushed. The same commit reports two lit and
six umbra nodes in the repository it was built in, and eleven penumbra in a
fresh clone that has no checkpoints at all. The probes, the cracks and the
sweep are the same in both.

## How the ranking works

Six factors, all printed next to the node so the number can be recomputed by
hand:

1. **Relation weight.** Direct caller 3, data flow 2, type consumer 2,
   transitive caller 1.5, co-change file 1.
2. **What depends on it.** Multiplied by `1 + log2(1 + dependents)`.
3. **How weakly it was seen.** Multiplied by 1.0 umbra, 0.7 echo,
   0.6 afterimage, 0.5 other penumbra tiers, 0 lit.
4. **Far field.** Multiplied by 1.5 across a package boundary.
5. **Fault line.** Multiplied by 1.5 when the call site sits inside error
   handling.
6. **Tests.** Plus 3 for a test function, plus 2 when a test reaches the node.

**The beacon override**: a call site within four lines of a `SAFETY`,
`CRITICAL` or `INVARIANT` comment is pinned to the top of the docket whatever
it scored, with the comment shown. Someone wrote that note by hand; it outranks
a heuristic.

**The scar factor** is opt in with `--history` and multiplies by up to 2 for a
file with several recent fix commits. It is off by default because it is noisy.

Ties break by file path then symbol name, so two runs on one checkpoint produce
the same order.

## The sweep

After the selected tests, the whole suite runs once by default. Every test that
changed state but was not selected is reported as a leak with the reason the
selection missed it: a path deeper than the search went, no resolved call edges
from the test file, a path only over a relation Umbra does not traverse, or
nothing the graph can see. The count is printed even when it is zero, because a
selection that audits itself is worth more than one that does not. `--no-audit`
skips it and the header says the selection is unaudited.

## Security

- Umbra runs as the invoking user and asks for nothing more. It sees exactly
  what you can see through git and the Entire CLI.
- **No transcript prose reaches any output**, with one named exception: the
  "session said" sentence, taken from Entire's stored checkpoint summary or, if
  there is none, the agent's own last sentence. It is scrubbed and capped at
  200 characters, and it is displayed, never verified.
- **Umbra never runs a command it found in a transcript.** Test ids are built
  from graph data, validated against `^[A-Za-z0-9_./:\[\]\-]+$`, and passed as
  separate argv elements. There is no `sh -c` anywhere in Umbra.
- The runner comes only from `--test`. Umbra echoes the full command before
  running it, and everything runs in detached worktrees, never in your working
  tree.
- The report is one self-contained file with a Content-Security-Policy that
  forbids external scripts, styles, images and connections. It makes no
  requests. The drop-in viewer on the landing page reads files in your browser
  and uploads nothing.
- Reports name symbols, files and spans inside the blast radius. Share one with
  the same care you would share a diff.

## Limitations

- Read evidence is file and line-range based. A mention in the agent's text is
  attention, not reading, and is ranked as the weakest tier.
- Graph edges are not complete: reflection, dynamic dispatch and configuration
  are invisible, so umbra is a **lower bound** on what was unexamined. The
  sweep's leak reasons are how a reader sees the gap.
- Fault lines and beacons are matched by a regular expression window around the
  call-site line, not by a parser.
- Ranking weights are hand set and printed. They are a heuristic, not a
  measurement.
- Scrubbing of command prefixes and failure excerpts is pattern based.
- One transcript adapter, for Claude Code. An agent whose transcript carries no
  tool records gets the unknown state.
- A destructive `--test` runner does what it says. The echo before execution is
  the only guard.
- **Worktrees are keyed by commit in a shared directory, so two checkouts of
  one repository collide on one worktree.** They are removed on exit unless
  `--keep-worktrees` was passed, but a run that died before its cleanup, or a
  checkout that has since been deleted, leaves one behind. A leftover is now
  reused only when it is a healthy checkout sitting at the wanted commit, and
  otherwise removed and pruned first, which covers the deleted-checkout case.
  What it does not cover is a healthy worktree belonging to a different
  checkout of the same repository: that one is reused, and it carries the other
  checkout's `.git` link with it, so if that checkout sits somewhere Graph
  refuses to run the failure lands in the run that did nothing wrong. There is
  no `umbra clean` command; `SECURITY_AND_ACCESS.md` describes one and it was
  never built. Delete them by hand:

  ```
  rm -rf "$ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR/wt"                  # managed install
  rm -rf "${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/umbra/wt"    # otherwise
  ```

  Under a managed install that first path is usually
  `~/.local/share/entire/plugins/data/umbra/wt`.
- **A check that has never been observed to fail is not yet a check.** Four
  verifications in this build returned a confident pass that was wrong: local
  tests green on a repository a clone could not build, a cracked-probe count
  that named a test outside the selection, a commit check that counted `ok`
  lines instead of looking for `FAIL`, and a refs audit that reported thirty
  refs of zero bytes because `git ls-tree` is scoped to the working directory.
  The clearest case had no symptom at all: all four label-placement tests are
  built on `Box.Overlaps`, and making it return false for every pair left every
  one of them passing, across all eight scenarios. They had been proving
  determinism, not collision. Every check named in this README now has a test
  that plants what the check is for and asserts it fires, and each of those was
  proved by mutating the code it checks until it failed. That is the standard;
  it is not a guarantee that nothing else here is passing for the wrong reason.
- The examined set is built from the session's tool activity. An agent that
  reads and edits through shell commands rather than through file tools leaves
  no read or edit event, so its work looks unexamined. Umbra found this in its
  own build; the report is in `umbra/site/self/`. Every report now carries a
  coverage line saying how many of the session's events were file reads and how
  many were shell commands, so a thin report can be told from a real finding.
- **The report's script is about 1215 lines against a design target of 700,**
  and its stylesheet about 480 against 400. Three things account for almost all
  of the excess and none of them were foreseen when the target was set: the
  attention replay carries a second implementation of the classifier, because
  the map has to be reconstructed at any point in the session and that means
  the state rules exist in Go and again in the browser; the day scheme and the
  print block are a second and third set of rules for the light field, since
  removing a glow on a light ground reads as more light rather than less; and
  the node shapes are drawn per state and per penumbra tier so the four states
  survive greyscale. The duplication of the classifier is the part worth
  regretting, and it is guarded rather than trusted: a test feeds eight
  recorded scenarios through both implementations at three playhead positions
  each and compares every state, tier and announcement.

## Not built, and why

Adapters for other agents (they get the unknown state, which is correct for a
transcript with no tool records). Subagent transcripts. Live mode during a
session and a blind-spot budget gate (shadow-branch data is not documented
output). Mutability analysis of callees (nothing in the documented surface
provides it). Coverage deltas (needs coverage tooling in the target
repository). Trend dashboards. Cross-repository dependents. And Umbra never
writes code: it shows the shadow, it does not fix it.

## Corrections to the design documents

Five places where the four planning documents in `umbra/docs/` describe
something the installed tools do not do. All five were forced by real output,
none by preference. The documents are the original design and are left as
written; these are the corrections the code carries.

1. **The checkpoint trailer is not hexadecimal.** ARCHITECTURE.md section 1
   describes `Entire-Checkpoint: <12 hex>`. The installed CLI writes a 26
   character ULID, for example `01M1PVD1WBK1J1J8GWDNJJR7XZ`. A hex-only pattern
   matched nothing, so every commit fell through to the session-window fallback
   while reporting, wrongly, that it carried no trailer. The pattern now takes
   alphanumeric ids of 6 to 40 characters, which covers the ULID, the 12 hex id
   of imported history and the 40 hex id of a carry-forward entry.

2. **`pytest -q` cannot be verified.** PRD.md uses it in the command surface
   and in the demo. Quiet mode prints no per-test ids, so `graph verify`
   answers `output format not recognised` and records zero results. The default
   is now `pytest -v`, and the table says `add -v` when a baseline comes back
   exit-code only.

3. **Flags after the reference were silently dropped.** The surface in PRD.md
   is `entire umbra <ref> [flags]`, but Go's flag package stops parsing at the
   first non-flag argument, so `entire umbra HEAD --run none` ignored
   `--run none` and then failed asking for a test runner. Argv is reordered
   before parsing, with boolean flags handled so they do not swallow the
   reference.

4. **`graph checkpoint` answers about the wrong commit when the pairing was a
   guess.** ARCHITECTURE.md calls it the documented bridge between Graph and
   Checkpoints, and `LoadSources` tried it first. It returns the changes of the
   commit *that checkpoint belongs to*. When a reference is paired with a
   checkpoint by session window, that is a guess about which session produced
   the commit and says nothing about which commit the checkpoint owns. This
   never showed here, because the pairing happens to choose an imported
   checkpoint that owns no commit and the fallback runs. In a clone it chose a
   hook-written checkpoint that does own one, and the report described that
   commit's changes under the header of the one the reader asked for: the
   header said `1c2cf29` while the sources were the transcript package from
   phase 3. The bridge is now used only when the reference resolved through the
   trailer or through the checkpoint id, where the two are the same work.

5. **A stale worktree poisoned every later run.** Worktrees are keyed by commit
   under a shared data directory, so two checkouts of one repository, or a run
   that died before its cleanup, collide on one path. The code reused anything
   with a `.git` in it. A worktree left behind by a checkout that had since
   been deleted made git unable to read its metadata and Graph refuse to run
   there, for every subsequent run against that commit from any checkout. A
   leftover is now reused only when it is a healthy checkout sitting at the
   wanted commit, and otherwise removed and pruned first. The residual case is
   in the limitations above.

Corrections 4 and 5 were both found by the end-to-end tests failing in a fresh
clone after passing here, which is the same lesson as the `.gitignore` below.

Two smaller ones, for completeness. Entire has more than one wording for an
absent summary, so any fully italicised summary block is treated as absent. And
`graph impact --format json` carries `call_site.line` and `additional_sites`
directly, so it is the primary path and the text parser the design sketched is
the fallback, still tested.

## The final review

Phase 11 was a semantic-diff review of the whole build to that point,
comparing the first commit against the last:

```
entire graph diff --base 2495309553ee8c01a61a3c4922e45861d3d4de6d --head HEAD --repo .
```

The diff itself is unremarkable: 1014 added entities, no signature changes, and
no function without an incoming edge, which is what a build that only ever added
code should look like. The interesting part was what the diff did not contain,
and it is the single most useful thing Graph did in this build.

### The .gitignore that hid the command package

Reading the diff, `umbra/cmd` was missing. Not thin, not partial: the graph had
no symbols for it at all, while it had 1014 for everything else. A directory of
Go files that the build had been compiling and testing for nine phases was, as
far as Graph could see, not there.

Graph builds its snapshot from the repository, and it honours `.gitignore`. So
the question was not what Graph had failed to parse. It was what git had been
told to ignore. The answer was the second line of a `.gitignore` I wrote myself
in the first commit, under a heading that says exactly what I meant it to do:

```
# Go build output
entire-umbra
```

I meant that to ignore the compiled binary, which is written as `entire-umbra`.
A gitignore pattern with no slash in it is not anchored to the repository root
and does not distinguish a file from a directory: it matches any path component
with that name, at any depth. The binary is called `entire-umbra`. So is the
directory the binary's source lives in. The pattern matched
`umbra/cmd/entire-umbra/` and everything under it.

`git ls-files umbra/cmd/` returned nothing. `main.go`, `analyze.go`,
`execute.go`, `options.go`, `output.go`, `record.go` and `options_test.go` had
never been committed. The command package went in during phase 2 and was
untracked through phase 10, nine phases in which every commit message reported
a rising test count that included tests in a file the repository did not have.

Nothing caught it, and nothing was going to. `go build ./...` and
`go test ./...` read the working tree, and the files were on disk, so they were
green throughout and told me nothing. `git status` says nothing about a path it
has been told to ignore. `git commit -a` does not add an ignored file. The only
symptom available to me was one I never looked at: a clone.

The fix was to anchor the patterns to the paths the binaries are actually
written to, so a directory name can never collide with them again:

```
/entire-umbra
/umbra/entire-umbra
/umbra-out/
```

The seven files were then committed, and the thing that should have been done
long before was done at last:

```
git clone . /tmp/clone && cd /tmp/clone/umbra
go build ./...   # OK
go test ./...    # every package ok
```

That clone is the verification. Before the fix it would have failed to build,
because `package main` did not exist in the repository. After it, it builds and
every test passes, which is the only evidence that means anything here.

This is the clearest case in the build of Graph driving a decision rather than
confirming one. Nothing else in the toolchain was looking at the repository.
The compiler, the test runner and my own reading were all looking at the
working tree, where the code was present and correct. Graph was looking at what
had actually been committed, and the gap between those two things was an entire
package. A green test run is not the same as a correct repository, and it takes
a tool that reads the repository to tell you which one you have.

### The self report

Then Umbra was run on the session that built it. On the commit where it changed
its own `shadow.Build`, all twelve dependents came back umbra, including every
scenario test. That reading is correct, and the reason is the most useful thing
this project learned about itself: the change was made with a shell command
rather than the editing tool, so the session produced no read and no edit event
for that file. **Umbra's examined set is built from tool activity, so an agent
that edits through the shell leaves no trace Umbra can see.** It is the same
shape of blind spot the product exists to find, pointed at the product. The
report is in `umbra/site/self/`.

Running the report on itself also found two bugs in the scrubber, both fixed:
paths from outside the repository were reaching the timeline through search
output, and the base64 heuristic was redacting git object ids and worktree
paths, which is exactly the text a reader needs in order to check a line.

## Development record

Umbra was built in a standalone repository, `u7k4rs6/Umbra`, rather than inside
a fork of `entireio/entire-graph`. The `umbra/` layout from ARCHITECTURE.md was
preserved exactly so the module can be grafted into a fork without moving a
file, and `scripts/graft.sh` does that graft, with a dry run, without pushing.
The build's own checkpoint trail lives in this repository under
`refs/entire/checkpoints/`, and the phase by phase record is the table at the
top of [umbra/NOTES.md](umbra/NOTES.md), which covers all seventeen phases and
carries what each one found and where the design documents turned out to be
wrong.

Seventeen phases, of which the first thirteen built the product. The last four
were not features:

- **14** replaced the landing page's scripted sample with a real run, added a
  second map from an imported session in another project, and prepared two
  scripts that were deliberately not executed: the graft, and a read-only audit
  of what the checkpoint refs on the remote contain.
- **15** made the scrubber the only exit. Five leaks had been the same bug five
  times, an output path that wrote without scrubbing, so the renderers now take
  a value that only the scrubbing path can produce. It also gave every check in
  the project a test that proves the check can fail.
- **16** restyled the landing page around a drawn eclipse. No raster asset and
  no request for one: the corona is inline SVG built deterministically from the
  report's own numbers.
- **17** is this pass: two visual checks decided from screenshots rather than
  from the CSS, [umbra/PUBLISH.md](umbra/PUBLISH.md), and the verification of
  this README against the repository.

[umbra/PUBLISH.md](umbra/PUBLISH.md) is a checklist for the sitting in which
this repository is made public. Nothing in it has been run.

**Which maps are which.** The landing page shows two, and they are not the same
kind of thing.

- The first is a **real session on a seeded fixture**. The session, its tool
  activity and the test results are real: checkpoint `b20f84567474` against
  commit `1c2cf29`, where an agent changed a signature and five probes cracked.
  What is arranged is the fixture underneath it, `umbra/fixtures/app`, which was
  written to have callers a session would plausibly miss. The sentence above the
  map is the agent's own, taken from the stored transcript.
- The second is **not seeded at all**: a real session from another project of
  the builder's, imported with `entire import` and analysed unchanged. Every one
  of the four symbols that depend on what it changed came back umbra. Nothing
  about it was arranged, including the result.

**Nothing on the page is scripted.** There is no map drawn from an invented
report. Until phase 14 there was one: the sample was assembled by the site
generator, with a checkpoint id of `sample000class`, a commit of all zeros and a
session sentence written by hand, under a caption calling it a real report. It
was replaced by a real run, and the generator now refuses a report carrying
those markers so the caption cannot drift away from the file again.

The eight scenarios under `umbra/fixtures/recorded/` are **authored
transcripts**, written to exercise one classifier rule each. They drive tests
and are never rendered as a map on the page. `umbra/fixtures/recorded/minimal/`
is different: a full recording of a real short session, hand reviewed before it
was committed.

## Prior work and AI disclosure

No code was reused. The idea of subtracting the examined set from a blast
radius was developed in planning for this event.

All product code across all seventeen phases was written during the build with
an AI coding agent, captured in Entire checkpoints. That includes the tests, the
landing page, the corona renderer and every document in this repository except
the four planning documents in `umbra/docs/`, which were written before the
build with AI assistance and are the first commit.

What came from the human rather than the agent: the problem, the four settled
decisions in the kickoff, the scope of each phase, the decision to keep the
repository private, and the visual direction for the landing page in phase 16,
which was specified before it was built and not proposed by the agent. Every
phase was reviewed and accepted by hand before the next one started.

`umbra/NOTES.md` records what the probe found, which degradations are in
effect, the places the design documents turned out to be wrong about the
installed tools, and the mistakes: the four confident wrong answers, the five
scrubbing leaks, and the label tests that were proving nothing. Those are in
there because a build record that only lists what worked is not a record.

## Layout

```
umbra/
  cmd/entire-umbra/     flags, wiring, exit codes
  internal/runner/      the one boundary to external processes, and its replay
  internal/checkpoint/  resolve, worktrees, transcript fetch
  internal/transcript/  normalized events; the Claude Code adapter
  internal/graph/       snapshot, relations, BFS, impact, commit, verify
  internal/shadow/      examined set, classifier, ranker, selection, forensics
  internal/report/      table, json, layout, html, packet
  fixtures/app/         the seeded Python service
  fixtures/recorded/    the eight scenarios, plus one real minimal recording
  scripts/              the graft and the read-only checkpoint refs audit
  site/                 landing page, the corona renderer, the drop-in viewer
  docs/                 the four planning documents, and docs/renders/
  NOTES.md              the phase by phase build record
  PUBLISH.md            the checklist for making this repository public
```

Built during Bengaluru Tech Week on the Entire ecosystem.

# Umbra — Track 2: Build with Graph Intelligence

## What it decides

Umbra turns an agent-authored change into an impact-aware code-review workflow:
it identifies changed definitions, follows their dependents through Entire
Graph, subtracts the code the checkpoint shows the agent examined, and ranks
the remaining shadow as review targets. It selects the tests that reach those
targets, runs them, and then runs a full-suite sweep to audit that selection.

The decision is actionable: review the ranked `umbra` nodes first and run the
tests attached to them before accepting the change.

## Graph evidence and verification

Each report preserves the evidence behind its recommendation:

- Changed definitions with source file and line span.
- Traversed graph relations, including callers, data-flow dependents, type
  consumers, imports, co-change files, and test reachability.
- Checkpoint-derived evidence of reads, edits, searches, and agent statements.
- Source locations, selected test identifiers, individual test results, and a
  full-suite leak check.

The HTML report is a replayable eclipse map; `umbra.packet.md` is the concise
review handoff; `umbra.json` is the inspectable machine-readable record.

## Run

Requirements: the Entire CLI with Checkpoints enabled, the Entire Graph plugin,
Go, and the test runner for the target repository.

```sh
go install github.com/u7k4rs6/Umbra/umbra/cmd/entire-umbra@main
entire umbra <checkpoint-id-or-commit> --test "pytest -v" --out ./umbra-out
open ./umbra-out/umbra.html
```

For the included seeded fixture:

```sh
cd umbra/fixtures/app && ./setup.sh && cd ../..
. umbra/fixtures/app/.venv/bin/activate
entire umbra 1c2cf29 --test "pytest -v" --out ./umbra-out
```

## Evidence artifacts

- `umbra/site/index.html` and `umbra/site/map.html`: static, inspectable demo.
- `umbra/site/sample/umbra.json`: seeded fixture report used by the demo.
- `umbra/site/self/umbra.html`: Umbra analyzing one of its own mapped commits.
- `umbra/fixtures/app`: source and tests for reproducing the seeded failure.

## Limits

Umbra is intentionally conservative: unavailable transcript evidence is shown
as `unknown`, not inferred. Graph relations that are unavailable or not
traversed are listed in the report. A selected-test pass is not treated as
proof; the full-suite sweep reports any missed failures as leaks.

95	## Where the documents turned out to be wrong
96	
97	Three corrections, all forced by real output rather than preference.
98	
99	1. **The checkpoint trailer is not hexadecimal.** ARCHITECTURE.md section 1
100	   describes `Entire-Checkpoint: <12 hex>`. The installed CLI writes a 26
101	   character ULID, for example `01M1PVD1WBK1J1J8GWDNJJR7XZ`. A hex-only pattern
102	   matched nothing and every commit fell through to the session-window
103	   fallback while reporting, wrongly, that the commit carried no trailer. The
104	   pattern now accepts alphanumeric ids of 6 to 40 characters, which covers the
105	   ULID, the 12 hex id of imported history and the 40 hex id of a carry-forward
106	   entry, and preserves case so `git log --grep` can match the exact text.
107	
108	2. **`pytest -q` cannot be verified.** PRD.md uses `pytest -q` in the command
109	   surface and in the 90-second demo. Quiet mode prints no per-test ids, so
110	   `graph verify` answers `output format not recognised` and records zero
111	   results. `pytest -v` parses cleanly. The default is now `pytest -v`, and the
112	   table says `add -v` when a baseline comes back exit-code only.
113	
114	3. **Flags after the reference were silently dropped.** The surface in PRD.md
115	   is `entire umbra <ref> [flags]`, but Go's flag package stops parsing at the
116	   first non-flag argument, so `entire umbra HEAD --run none` ignored
117	   `--run none` and failed asking for a test runner. Argv is now reordered
118	   before parsing, with boolean flags handled so they do not swallow the
119	   reference.

121	Two smaller ones:
122	
123	- Entire has more than one wording for an absent summary. Imported checkpoints
124	  say `*No summary...*` and hook-written ones say `*Not generated yet...*`.
125	  Any fully italicised block is now treated as absent.
126	- `graph impact --format json` is better than the text shape the design
127	  sketched, because it carries `call_site.line` and `additional_sites`
128	  directly. It is now the primary path; the text parser is the fallback and is

172	## Honest limits of this particular demo
173	
174	The exposure comes from the checkpoint of the session that built Umbra, which
175	is one long session covering the whole build rather than a short session that
176	ends at the commit. Two consequences show in the output above:
177	
178	- The session-said line falls back to the last thing the agent said, which is a
179	  sentence of narration rather than a commit summary. In a short session ending
180	  at a commit it would be the closing account of the change. The fallback is
181	  bounded by the last edit to a source file where it can be, and the header
182	  always names where the sentence came from.
183	- Files touched anywhere in the long session are lit for every commit in it, so
184	  the illumination fraction is not comparable to a short session's.
185	
186	The dedicated recorded scenarios in phase 7 are the fix for both, and the
187	fixture is disclosed as seeded in PRD.md.

259	
260	The semantic diff reported **no symbols at all** for `umbra/cmd`. The cause was
261	a `.gitignore` pattern I wrote in phase 0: an unanchored `entire-umbra`, meant
262	for the built binary, also matches the source directory `cmd/entire-umbra/`.
263	The whole command package was untracked for nine phases. Local tests passed the
264	entire time because the files were on disk. A fresh clone would not have built.
265	
266	This is the single most useful thing the build produced: a green test run is
267	not the same as a correct repository, and only a tool that looks at the
268	repository rather than the working tree could tell the difference.
269	
270	Running Umbra on its own build then found a limitation worth stating rather
271	than tuning away. On the commit where Umbra changed `shadow.Build`, all twelve
272	dependents came back umbra, including every scenario test. The reading is
273	correct: that change was made with a shell command rather than the editing
274	tool, so the session produced no read and no edit event for the file. **Umbra's
275	examined set is built from tool activity, so an agent that works through the
276	shell leaves no trace it can see.** It is in the README's limitations and in
277	`site/self/`.

279	That self run also found two scrubber bugs:
280	
281	- Paths from outside the repository reached the timeline through search output.
282	  A path outside the repository can never match a symbol in the field, so it is
283	  noise, and carrying it out leaks the layout of the machine. Such paths are now
284	  dropped at the adapter.
285	- The base64 heuristic redacted git object ids and worktree paths, because a
286	  forty character hex sha matches the base64 shape and the character class
287	  included the slash. The reproduce list is only useful if a reader can check a
288	  line, so hex runs are exempt and the slash is out of the class.

341	### Phase 12: the fresh minimal record
342	
343	`fixtures/recorded/minimal/recording.json` is now committed: a full Runner
344	recording of a short real session on the fixture app. The session read
345	`app/models.py` in full, read `app/refunds.py` with an offset and limit that
346	stop before `apply_refund`, searched for `round_money`, changed that one

349	
350	**The 900 KB recording of the build session is deliberately not committed, and
351	this is why.** A full recording embeds the checkpoint transcript, and for this
352	repository that transcript is the entire build session. `umbra record` scrubs
353	it, so absolute paths, the user and host name, the author name, the email
354	address and token shapes are all gone. But SECURITY_AND_ACCESS.md requires a
355	fixture recording to be **hand reviewed** before it is committed, and 900 KB of
356	conversation cannot honestly be read line by line. Committing it and saying it
357	was reviewed would be exactly the kind of unchecked claim this project exists
358	to catch. The minimal recording is twelve transcript records; it was actually
359	read end to end, record by record, and that reading is what the rule asks for.
360	
361	Two things had to be worked out to get a recording worth committing:
362	
363	1. **Where it was recorded from.** Taken inside the Umbra repository the same
364	   short session produces **3.8 MB**, of which **3.4 MB is one `graph snapshot`
365	   of the whole codebase**. None of that bulk says anything about the session.
366	   Recorded against a repository holding only the fixture app it is **135 KB**.
367	   The session's paths were relocated to that root; every tool call, range,
368	   result and timestamp is the real one, and the scrub replaces the prefix with
369	   `<repo>` in any case.
370	
371	2. **Graph refuses a worktree under a restricted path.** With the fixture
372	   repository in the session scratch directory, `graph commit` answered
373	   `refuse Git subprocesses for unsafe or unreadable repository metadata`,
374	   because the worktree metadata pointed into a directory it could not treat as
375	   safe. Moving the repository under `$HOME` fixed it. Worth knowing before
376	   anyone tries to record from a temporary directory.
377	
378	**The hand review found a real scrubber gap.** The first recording contained
379	the repository owner's real name and email address, from the author line that
380	`checkpoint explain --short` prints and Umbra reads for the session-said
381	sentence. The scrubber had no rule for an email address and no way to know a
382	display name. Both are fixed: an email pattern is always redacted, and
383	`umbra record` now asks git for the author names configured in the repository
384	and removes them by value, since a name cannot be recognised by shape. The
385	author line in the committed recording reads `author   <author> <<redacted>>`.
386	
387	Checks that now run as tests: the recording replays every call it holds, it
388	contains the calls a real analysis makes, and it carries no absolute home path,
389	email address or token shape while still showing the `<repo>` and `<home>`
390	placeholders that prove the scrub ran rather than found nothing.

504	### Phase 13: what the end to end tests found by failing in a clone
505	
506	The exit-code tests passed here and failed the moment they ran in a fresh
507	clone. That is the phase 11 lesson again, and this time it surfaced two product
508	bugs and one piece of fragility in the test itself.
509	
510	**1. `graph checkpoint` was answering about the wrong commit.** `LoadSources`
511	tries `graph checkpoint <id>` first, because ARCHITECTURE.md calls it the
512	documented bridge between Graph and Checkpoints. But it returns the changes of
513	the commit *that checkpoint belongs to*. When a reference is paired with a
514	checkpoint by session window, that is a guess about which session produced the
515	commit and says nothing about which commit the checkpoint owns. In this working
516	copy the pairing happens to choose an imported checkpoint, which has no commit,
517	so the fallback runs and the report is correct. In a clone it chose a
518	hook-written checkpoint that does own a commit, and the report described that
519	commit's changes under the header of the one the reader asked for: the header
520	said `1c2cf29` while the sources were the transcript package from phase 3. The
521	bridge is now used only when the reference resolved through the trailer or
522	through the checkpoint id, where the two are the same piece of work.
523	
524	**2. A stale worktree poisoned every later run.** Worktrees are keyed by commit
525	under a shared data directory, so two checkouts of one repository, or a run
526	that died before its cleanup, collide on the same path. The code reused
527	anything with a `.git` in it. A worktree left behind by a checkout that had
528	since been deleted made git unable to read its metadata and Graph refuse to run
529	there, for every subsequent run against that commit from any checkout. A
530	leftover is now reused only when it is a healthy checkout sitting at the wanted
531	commit, and otherwise removed and pruned first.
532	
533	**3. The tests were asserting on states that are not repository state.** They
534	checked that a given commit has umbra nodes. Node states come from the examined
535	set, which comes from whichever checkpoint the reference pairs with, and the
536	set of checkpoints present differs between a working copy and a clone: imported
537	history is local and is not pushed. The same commit reports six umbra nodes
538	here and none in a clone, both correct. The tests now run the binary once,
539	read the summary from its JSON, and derive a condition that must fire from what
540	the report actually says. They also skip when the toolchain cannot analyse the
541	checkout at all, which happens where Graph refuses to run git, the same
542	restriction phase 12 hit when recording from a temporary directory.
543	
544	Verified in three places before the commit: this working copy, a clone under
545	`$HOME`, and a clone under the restricted scratch directory, where the suite
546	skips cleanly rather than failing.

625	## Phase 15: the scrubber becomes the only exit
626	
627	Five scrubbing bugs so far have been the same bug five times: an output path
628	that wrote without going through the scrubber. Each was fixed where it was
629	found, which fixed that path and left the shape intact.
630	
631	| # | Phase | The path that wrote unscrubbed |
632	|---|---|---|
633	| 1 | 11 | Paths from outside the repository reached the timeline through search output |
634	| 2 | 11 | The base64 heuristic redacted git object ids and worktree paths, so the reproduce list could not be checked |
635	| 3 | 12 | The recording carried an email address; the scrubber had no rule for one |
636	| 4 | 14.1 | `graph.Verify` appended its commands to `a.Commands` raw, bypassing the scrubber every other command went through |
637	| 5 | 14.2 | Only `umbra record` set `scrub.Names`, so an ordinary run left the author's display name in the timeline |
638	
639	Number 2 is the odd one out: it removed too much rather than too little. The
640	other four are the same shape.
641	
642	### The inventory, before anything changed
643	
644	Every place an artifact is written, and whether it scrubbed:
645	
646	| Writer | What it writes | Scrubbed before phase 15 |
647	|---|---|---|
648	| `emit` stdout, `--format table` | terminal table | only whatever the builder happened to scrub |
649	| `emit` stdout, `--format json` | report JSON | same |
650	| `emit` stdout, `--format packet` | packet markdown | same |
651	| `emit --out`, `umbra.json` | report JSON | same |
652	| `emit --out`, `umbra.packet.md` | packet markdown | same |
653	| `emit --out`, `umbra.html` | map, with the JSON embedded | same |
654	| `report.BuildLayout` via `emit` | node and ring label text inside the map | **no**, it ran before any scrub and copied node names into the layout |
655	| `runner.Recorder.Save` | `fixtures/recorded/*/recording.json` | yes, but through a nil-able function, and `--no-scrub` turned it off |
656	| `gen-site` | `site/umbra.css`, `site/umbra.js` | not applicable, they are source assets |
657	| `gen-site` `embedSample` | the JSON embedded in `site/index.html` | **no check of its own**, it inherited whatever the committed sample carried |
658	| `analyze.go` | the reproduce list | yes, since 14.1 |
659	| `execute.go` | the verify commands in the reproduce list | yes, since 14.1 |
660	
661	"Only whatever the builder happened to scrub" is the honest description of the
662	old state. Values were scrubbed as they were built, one call site at a time,
663	and the renderers took an `*Analysis` and wrote whatever was in it. Nothing in
664	the type system knew the difference between an analysis that had been through
665	the scrubber and one that had not.
666	
667	### The choke point
668	
669	`report.Sealed` wraps an `*Analysis` in an unexported field. `report.Seal` is
670	the only way to make one, and `WriteJSON`, `MarshalJSON`, `HTML`, `Packet` and
671	`Table` all take a `Sealed` and refuse a zero value. `BuildJSON` is now
672	`buildJSON` and unexported. A new output path cannot skip the scrubber by
673	omission, because there is nothing for it to write from until it has sealed
674	something.
675	
676	`Seal` scrubs every string in the analysis that could carry text from the
677	machine, then builds the layout from the scrubbed values. That ordering is the
678	fix for the row marked no above: the layout carries node names and file names
679	as label text, and building it first meant a scrubbed report could ship with an
680	unscrubbed picture on it. Nothing had leaked that way yet. It was open.
681	
682	A nil scrubber means the default one for this machine, never no scrubbing.
683	There is no flag for less. `umbra record --no-scrub` is gone: a recording is
684	committed, and a flag that turns off scrubbing on a committed artifact is the
685	next bug in the table above waiting for someone to forget it.
686	
687	### One derivation of the scrub inputs
688	
689	`Options.Scrubber` derives home, repository, user, host and the git author
690	names once and caches them on the options. `umbra record` and the analysis
691	pipeline both call it and get the same value. Bug 5 was possible only because
692	there were two constructions and one of them was missing a line.
693	
694	### The output-wide check
695	
696	`report.ScanArtifact` reads finished bytes and reports absolute home paths,
697	addresses, token shapes and supplied display names, with line numbers. It does
698	not care which code path produced the bytes, which is the point: a new writer
699	is covered the day it exists rather than the day someone adds it to a list.
700	
701	`TestNoGeneratedArtifactCarriesAnythingPrivate` walks `site/`,
702	`fixtures/recorded/` and `docs/renders/` rather than naming files, and takes
703	the author names from `git log` so it fails for whoever cloned the repository
704	as readily as for its author. **It scans 25 artifacts and found nothing.** The
705	existing corpus needed no re-scrubbing, and the self report regenerated through
706	the sealed pipeline is byte-identical to the committed one.
707	
708	`gen-site` now runs the same scan before embedding either sample, so a report
709	produced by an older build or edited by hand cannot reach the landing page.

770	## Phase 16: the eclipse hero
771	
772	The landing page is restyled around a drawn total eclipse. Nothing in the
773	report, the report template, the drop-in viewer's behaviour or any Go file
774	changed. The new files are `site/landing.css`, `site/corona.js` and a rewritten
775	`site/index.html` and `site/site.js`. `site/umbra.css` and `site/umbra.js` are
776	still the report's own, copied by `gen-site`, and still byte-identical to it.
777	
778	### The corona is a renderer
779	
780	There is no raster asset on the page and no request for one. `corona.js` builds
781	the eclipse in inline SVG: layered radial gradients warped by a `feTurbulence`
782	`fractalNoise` with a fixed seed through an `feDisplacementMap`, streamers laid
783	along the x axis and rotated to their angles, an occluding disc taken out by a
784	mask, a bright ring hugging the limb, and one bright limb point with an
785	anisotropic flare made from a rotated linear gradient and one blur.
786	
787	It is deterministic. Nothing calls `Math.random`. The limb angle comes from a
788	hash of the checkpoint's commit and the streamer geometry from a small linear
789	generator seeded by the same number, so the same `umbra.json` always draws the
790	same corona. The filament count reads the report: twenty, plus forty six times
791	the lit fraction, plus three per source. More of the field in the light means a
792	denser corona, and the number comes from `summary`, not from a constant chosen
793	because it looked good.
794	
795	Cost was a real constraint, not a note. Every filter has an explicit
796	`filterUnits="userSpaceOnUse"` region, so it rasterises once at a fixed size.
797	No filter primitive is ever animated. The only thing that moves after the first
798	paint is a clip inset and an opacity. The day layer is a second copy of the
799	same two SVGs, so it would rasterise the turbulence twice; it is therefore
800	built only when the divider is off its resting position, which means an
801	ordinary visit pays for one corona.
802	
803	Four attempts, each judged from a screenshot rather than from the code:
804	
805	1. Uniform thick filaments over a strong body read as a cartoon sunburst, and
806	   the brightest part of the gradient sat *inside* the moon where nothing could
807	   see it.
808	2. Peaking the gradient at the limb fixed that and produced a visible circular
809	   rim at the outer edge.
810	3. Softening the tail moved the rim but did not remove it. The cause was that
811	   the outer stops were written as multiples of the limb radius, so the last
812	   one fell past the end of the gradient and the alpha dropped from 0.012 to
813	   zero inside the final one percent of the radius. Writing the tail in
814	   absolute fractions removed it.
815	4. The limb flare was drawn on top of the moon and read as a scratch across the
816	   disc. It is now drawn behind the moon, with only the bead in front, which is
817	   also what actually happens.
818	
819	### The hero is the live map wearing the eclipse
820	
821	The map is the same `renderInto` from `umbra.js`, drawn from the layout already
822	in `umbra.json`. The JS still computes no positions. The occluding disc sits at
823	the layout centre, so the four changed symbols are inside it and their
824	dependents sit in the corona at ring radii the Go code chose.
825	
826	One thing had to give. The map paints its own background rectangle in
827	`--night`, as the spec requires, and that rectangle covered the corona behind
828	it. The rectangle is made transparent by a CSS rule on the landing page and the
829	stage carries the ground colour instead. `umbra.js` is untouched; a CSS `fill`
830	outranks the presentation attribute it sets.
831	
832	### The four beats
833	
834	`01 CLAIM`, `02 FIELD`, `03 THE CUT`, `04 SWEEP`, in the project's own words.
835	Each drives the map to a real point in the timeline: seq 0, the last event
836	before the cut, `t0` itself, and the end. The page loads at `04`, which is the
837	eclipse, so nothing moves before first paint.

839	The beats drive the map **through the replay strip's own controls**: they click
840	a tick or send the key the strip already listens for. The landing page does not

843	### Day and night
844	
845	The divider is a real inversion, not a filter. The day side is a second drawing
846	of the same two SVGs under day tokens, clipped by `clip-path`, so its gradients
847	and pools are computed from day values and the shadow pools stay darker than
848	the paper around them. Cloning needed one thing that is easy to miss: duplicate
849	ids in one document resolve to whichever came first, so the day copy would have
850	pointed at the night layer's gradients and inherited the night palette. Every

853	It is a `role="slider"`, operable with the arrow keys, and it settles to
854	whichever scheme it was left nearest. `Home`, `End` and `Space` are stopped at
